notes.front: What is the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model?
notes.back: A reference model that splits network communication into seven layers, from the Physical Layer (1) up to the Application Layer (7).
notes.explanation: Each layer uses the services of the layer below and offers services to the layer above, so each can be described and standardised on its own.
notes.source: ITU-T Rec. X.200 (1994) | ISO/IEC 7498-1, OSI Basic Reference Model, §6.1
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like a seven-storey office where each floor handles one part of sending a parcel, but for network traffic.

notes.front: What is the TCP/IP model?
notes.back: The Internet's layered model of four layers (application, transport, IP and hardware) that work together to move data between hosts.
notes.explanation: Data passes down through the layers on the sender, each adding information, crosses the physical network, then passes back up on the receiver.
notes.evidence: TCP/IP communications are composed of four layers that work together to transfer data between hosts.
notes.source: SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2 Overview of Firewall Technologies
notes.example: Like the OSI model's seven floors squeezed into a four-storey building.

notes.front: What is an Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) address?
notes.back: A 32-bit address, usually written as four decimal numbers of 8 bits each separated by dots (dotted decimal).
notes.explanation: Each of the four numbers stands for one 8-bit octet, so every number lies between 0 and 255.
notes.evidence: Each IPv4 address is typically 32 bits long and is written as four decimal numbers representing 8-bit octets and separated by decimal points or periods.
notes.source: SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, §2.3.1 Extended Address Space
notes.example: Like a four-part street address such as 10.20.30.40, where each part is a number from 0 to 255.

notes.front: What is an Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) address?
notes.back: A 128-bit address written as eight 16-bit fields in hexadecimal, separated by colons.
notes.explanation: The much longer address gives an enormous number of unique addresses compared with the 32-bit IPv4 space.
notes.evidence: Each IPv6 address is 128 bits long (as defined in RFC 4291) and is written as eight 16-bit fields in colon-delimited hexadecimal notation
notes.source: SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, §2.3.1 Extended Address Space
notes.example: Like IPv4, but with eight colon-separated hex groups such as 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:0000:0000:0001.

notes.front: What is the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP)?
notes.back: A transport-layer protocol giving a reliable, connection-oriented service with end-to-end reliability, resequencing and flow control.
notes.explanation: The layer beneath it gives no delivery guarantees, so reliable delivery, when needed, is left to the layers above it, such as TCP.
notes.source: RFC 1122, Requirements for Internet Hosts: Communication Layers, §1.1.3 Internet Protocol Suite
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.example: Like recorded post with numbered envelopes, but the receiver puts the pieces back in order and asks for any that go missing.

notes.front: In networking, what does a destination port number identify?
notes.back: Generally, the service listening on the destination host.
notes.explanation: Ports belong to the transport layer; the destination port picks out which listening service on the host the traffic is meant for.
notes.evidence: The transport layer may also include the notion of ports— a destination port number generally identifies a service listening on the destination host
notes.source: SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2 Overview of Firewall Technologies
notes.example: Like a flat number in a block of flats: the street address finds the building, the number finds the right door.

notes.front: What is a virtual private network (VPN)?
notes.back: A virtual network built on top of existing physical networks that provides a secure way to send data and control information between computers or networks.
notes.explanation: Because it rides on networks that already exist, such as the internet, it lets sensitive data cross public networks securely.
notes.evidence: A VPN is a virtual network built on top of existing physical networks that provides a secure communications mechanism for data and control information transmitted between computers or networks.
notes.source: SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Executive Summary
notes.example: Like a sealed private corridor built inside a busy public shopping centre.

notes.front: What is Internet Protocol Security (IPsec)?
notes.back: A framework of open standards for private communications over Internet Protocol networks; a widely used network-layer security control.
notes.explanation: Its most common use is to provide virtual private network services.
notes.evidence: IPsec is a framework of open standards for ensuring private communications over Internet Protocol (IP) networks.
notes.source: SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Abstract
notes.example: Like shrink-wrapping every parcel that leaves the depot, whatever is inside it.

notes.front: What is Transport Layer Security (TLS)?
notes.back: A cryptographic protocol that provides end-to-end communications security over networks, used for Internet communications and online transactions.
notes.explanation: NIST's control catalogue gives TLS as an example of how remote access sessions and online transactions can be protected while the data crosses networks.
notes.evidence: Transport Layer Security (TLS) is an example of a cryptographic protocol that provides end-to-end communications security over networks and is used for Internet communications and online transactions.
notes.source: SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-17(2) Remote Access | Protection of Confidentiality and Integrity Using Encryption
notes.example: Like a padlocked pouch for one conversation between a browser and a shop's website.

notes.front: In the OSI model, what is layer 1 called, and what does it provide?
notes.back: The Physical Layer: the mechanical, electrical, functional and procedural means to activate, maintain and deactivate physical connections that carry bits.
notes.explanation: It is the bottom of the stack; the Data Link Layer builds its connections on top of these physical connections.
notes.source: ITU-T Rec. X.200 (1994), §7.7.2 Physical Layer: Purpose
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the OSI model, what is layer 2 called, and what error-related job does it do?
notes.back: The Data Link Layer; it detects, and possibly corrects, errors that may occur in the Physical Layer.
notes.explanation: A data-link connection is built on one or more physical connections, so it is the first layer able to catch the errors those connections introduce.
notes.source: ITU-T Rec. X.200 (1994), §7.6.2 Data Link Layer: Purpose
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the OSI model, what is layer 3 called, and what does it spare the layer above from?
notes.back: The Network Layer; it carries data between the Transport Layers on each side, so the Transport Layer need not deal with routing across networks.
notes.explanation: It offers transmission in connectionless or connection mode, so the Transport Layer need not know how data finds its way across networks.
notes.source: ITU-T Rec. X.200 (1994), §7.5.2 Network Layer: Purpose
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the OSI model, what is layer 4 called, and what does it give the Session Layer?
notes.back: The Transport Layer; it moves data between the Session Layers on each side, reliably and cost-effectively, hiding how that transfer is achieved.
notes.explanation: It makes the best use of the network service beneath it to give each session the performance it needs at minimum cost.
notes.source: ITU-T Rec. X.200 (1994), §7.4.2 Transport Layer: Purpose
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the OSI model, what is layer 5 called, and what does it do?
notes.back: The Session Layer; it lets the two communicating sides organise and synchronise their dialogue and manage their data exchange.
notes.explanation: To do this it sets up a session connection, supports orderly exchanges over it, and releases it in an orderly way.
notes.source: ITU-T Rec. X.200 (1994), §7.3.2 Session Layer: Purpose
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the OSI model, what is layer 6 called, and what does it do?
notes.back: The Presentation Layer; it gives the applications on each side a common representation of the data they exchange.
notes.explanation: Each application can keep its own local data format, because this layer takes care of the shared form used between them; the standard calls this syntax independence.
notes.source: ITU-T Rec. X.200 (1994), §7.2.2 Presentation Layer: Purpose
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: In the OSI model, what is layer 7 called, and what makes it special?
notes.back: The Application Layer; as the highest layer, it is an application process's only way into OSI communication.
notes.explanation: Being at the top, it has no boundary with any higher layer; every lower layer serves it.
notes.source: ITU-T Rec. X.200 (1994), §7.1.2 Application Layer: Purpose
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the application layer of the TCP/IP model do?
notes.back: It sends and receives data for particular applications, such as name lookup, web and email protocols.
notes.explanation: It is the top of the four layers, and it can hold its own internal layers of protocols, one wrapped inside another.
notes.evidence: Application Layer. This layer sends and receives data for particular applications, such as Domain Name System (DNS), Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), and Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP).
notes.source: SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2 Overview of Firewall Technologies

notes.front: Which TCP/IP layer provides connection-oriented or connectionless services and can optionally ensure reliability?
notes.back: The transport layer.
notes.explanation: It carries application-layer services between networks; TCP is one of the protocols commonly used here.
notes.evidence: Transport Layer. This layer provides connection-oriented or connectionless services for transporting application layer services between networks, and can optionally ensure communications reliability.
notes.source: SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2 Overview of Firewall Technologies

notes.front: Which TCP/IP layer, also known as the network layer, routes packets across networks?
notes.back: The IP layer.
notes.explanation: IPv4 is its fundamental protocol, with IPv6 among the others commonly used there.
notes.evidence: IP Layer (also known as the Network Layer). This layer routes packets across networks. Internet Protocol version 4 (IPv4) is the fundamental network layer protocol for TCP/IP.
notes.source: SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2 Overview of Firewall Technologies

notes.front: Which TCP/IP layer, also known as the data link layer, handles communications on the physical network components?
notes.back: The hardware layer.
notes.explanation: It is the lowest of the four layers; Ethernet is its best-known protocol.
notes.evidence: Hardware Layer (also known as the Data Link Layer). This layer handles communications on the physical network components. The best known data link layer protocol is Ethernet.
notes.source: SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2 Overview of Firewall Technologies

notes.front: Which two OSI layers does the TCP/IP application layer essentially combine?
notes.back: The Presentation Layer (6) and the Application Layer (7).
notes.explanation: The Internet suite does not split its application layer further, though some of its application protocols have internal sub-layers of their own.
notes.source: RFC 1122, Requirements for Internet Hosts: Communication Layers, §1.1.3 Internet Protocol Suite
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: What does the subnet mask that goes with an IPv4 address denote?
notes.back: How many high-order bits of the address belong to the network address; the remaining lower-order bits identify the node.
notes.explanation: One 32-bit address therefore carries two things at once: which network, and which host on it.
notes.evidence: subnet mask, which denotes how many high-order bits of the address are assigned to the network address (RFC 950). The remaining lower-order bits are used to identify the node.
notes.source: SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, §3.1.5 IPv4 Addressing

notes.front: An IPv6 address is split into two portions. What are they, and what does each identify?
notes.back: The network prefix, which designates the host's network; and the host identifier, which identifies the node or interface on that network.
notes.explanation: The prefix can change, for example when a device moves, while the host identifier can stay the same.
notes.evidence: The network prefix designates the network upon which the host bearing the address resides. The host identifier identifies the node or interface within the network upon which it resides. The network prefix may change while the host identifier can remain static.
notes.source: SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, §2.3.1 Extended Address Space

notes.front: How can an IPv6 address be shortened when some of its colon-separated groups are all zeros?
notes.back: The all-zero groups can be compressed so that nothing appears between the colons (a double colon, ::).
notes.explanation: Leading zeros inside a group may also be dropped, but trailing zeros may not, because they hold place value.
notes.evidence: Any colon-delimited portion of an address containing all zeros may be compressed so that nothing appears between the leading and trailing colons.
notes.source: SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, §3.1 IPv6 address notation

notes.front: IPsec is a mandatory part of an IPv6 implementation; however, its use is {{c1::not required}}.
notes.explanation: Every IPv6 implementation must include IPsec, but whether traffic actually uses it is still a choice.
notes.evidence: IPsec is a mandatory part of an IPv6 implementation; however, its use is not required.
notes.source: SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, §2.3 (IPsec)

notes.front: How do IPv4 and IPv6 differ in address length, and what does that mean for the number of addresses?
notes.back: IPv4 uses 32 bits; IPv6 uses 128 bits, giving an enormously larger number of unique addresses.
notes.explanation: NIST puts the 128-bit space at enough for many trillions of addresses for every person on the planet.
notes.evidence: This new 128-bit address space provides an enormous number of unique addresses
notes.source: SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, §2.3.1 Extended Address Space

notes.front: What does the source port number in a transport-layer header usually identify?
notes.back: The port on the source host that the destination host should reply to.
notes.explanation: The destination port picks the service; the source port tells the destination where to send its reply.
notes.evidence: a source port usually identifies the port number on the source host that the destination host should reply to.
notes.source: SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2 Overview of Firewall Technologies

notes.front: How does TCP differ from the User Datagram Protocol, the other main Internet transport protocol?
notes.back: TCP is reliable and connection-oriented; the User Datagram Protocol is a connectionless (datagram) service.
notes.explanation: The Internet host requirements name these two as the primary transport protocols of the suite, while noting that others exist.
notes.source: RFC 1122, Requirements for Internet Hosts: Communication Layers, §1.1.3 Internet Protocol Suite
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words

notes.front: A VPN can provide confidentiality, integrity, data origin authentication, {{c1::replay protection}} and access control.
notes.explanation: Confidentiality is only one item: the guide also lists integrity, data origin authentication, replay protection and access control.
notes.evidence: A VPN can provide several types of data protection, including confidentiality, integrity, data origin authentication, replay protection, and access control.
notes.source: SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Executive Summary

notes.front: Which VPN architecture protects communications between two specific networks?
notes.back: Gateway-to-gateway.
notes.explanation: The guide's examples are an organisation's main office and branch office networks, or the networks of two business partners.
notes.evidence: Gateway-to-gateway. This architecture protects communications between two specific networks
notes.source: SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Executive Summary

notes.front: What other name does the remote access VPN architecture have, and what does it protect?
notes.back: Host-to-gateway; it protects communications between one or more individual hosts and a specific organisational network.
notes.explanation: It is most often used by hosts on unsecured networks that need to reach internal organisational services.
notes.evidence: Remote access. Also known as host-to-gateway, this architecture protects communications between one or more individual hosts and a specific network belonging to an organization.
notes.source: SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Executive Summary

notes.front: Which VPN architecture protects communication between two specific computers?
notes.back: Host-to-host.
notes.explanation: The guide suggests it when a few users must use or administer a remote system that needs inherently insecure protocols.
notes.evidence: A host-to-host architecture protects communication between two specific
notes.source: SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Executive Summary

notes.front: Why can a network-layer control such as IPsec protect traffic without changes to applications?
notes.back: Network-layer controls apply to all applications and are not application-specific.
notes.explanation: All communication between two hosts or networks can be protected at this layer, avoiding the difficulty of adding controls to each application.
notes.evidence: Controls at this layer apply to all applications and are not applicationspecific. For example, all network communications between two hosts or networks can be protected at this layer without modifying any applications on the clients or the servers.
notes.source: SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, §2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security

notes.front: What does a transport-layer control such as TLS protect, and what is the current best practice for TCP streams?
notes.back: The data in a single session between two hosts (a netflow); TLS is the current best practice for protecting TCP streams.
notes.explanation: TLS typically needs each application to support it, but far less customisation than application-layer controls.
notes.evidence: Controls at this layer can be used to protect the data in a single communication session between two hosts, often called a netflow.
notes.source: SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, §2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security

notes.front: What can a network-layer control like IPsec protect that a transport-layer control like TLS cannot?
notes.back: The Internet Protocol information in each packet, which is added at the network layer, below TLS.
notes.explanation: The guide's reason is where the information is added: at the network layer, beneath the layer where TLS works.
notes.evidence: Because IP information is added at the network layer, transport layer controls cannot protect it.
notes.source: SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, §2.1 The Need for Network Layer Security

notes.front: A mainframe and a tablet store text in different character encodings, yet exchange records correctly because one layer gives both a common representation of the data. In the OSI model, which layer is doing that work?
notes.back: C: The Presentation Layer (6).
notes.explanation: Giving the applications on each side a common representation of the data they exchange, so each can keep its own local format, is the Presentation Layer's purpose.
notes.source: ITU-T Rec. X.200 (1994), §7.2.2 Presentation Layer: Purpose
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.choices:
A) The Session Layer (5)
B) The Transport Layer (4)
C) The Presentation Layer (6)
D) The Data Link Layer (2)
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because the Session Layer organises and synchronises dialogue, not data representation. B is wrong because the Transport Layer moves data between the Session Layers on each side without changing how it is represented. D is wrong because the Data Link Layer deals with errors from the physical connections.

notes.front: A developer writes the part of a chat program that formats and sends each message for the chat service. In the TCP/IP model, which layer does this code belong to?
notes.back: C: The application layer.
notes.explanation: Sending and receiving data for a particular application is the application layer's job; the layers below only carry, route and physically transmit it.
notes.evidence: Application Layer. This layer sends and receives data for particular applications
notes.source: SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2 Overview of Firewall Technologies
notes.choices:
A) The IP layer
B) The transport layer
C) The application layer
D) The hardware layer
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because the transport layer carries application services between networks rather than handling one application's data. A is wrong because the IP layer routes packets. D is wrong because the hardware layer handles the physical network components.

notes.front: A firewall log shows four source addresses. Which one is an IPv6 address?
notes.explanation: IPv6 addresses are written as eight 16-bit groups in hexadecimal separated by colons; IPv4 addresses are four decimal numbers separated by dots.
notes.evidence: Each IPv6 address is 128 bits long (as defined in RFC 4291) and is written as eight 16-bit fields in colon-delimited hexadecimal notation
notes.source: SP 800-119, Guidelines for the Secure Deployment of IPv6, §2.3.1 Extended Address Space
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D are wrong because each is four decimal numbers from 0 to 255 separated by dots, which is the dotted-decimal IPv4 form.

notes.front: A server runs both a web service and a file-transfer service on the same address. An administrator wants a firewall to block only the file-transfer service. Which value in incoming traffic best tells the two services apart?
notes.back: B: The destination port number.
notes.explanation: Both services share one address, and a destination port number generally identifies which service on the destination host the traffic is for.
notes.evidence: a destination port number generally identifies a service listening on the destination host
notes.source: SP 800-41 Rev. 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, §2 Overview of Firewall Technologies
notes.choices:
A) The destination address
B) The destination port number
C) The source port number
D) The subnet mask
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong because both services sit behind the same destination address. C is wrong because the source port usually names where replies should go on the sender. D is wrong because a subnet mask only splits an address into network and node parts.

notes.front: A payroll system sends salary files that must arrive complete and in the right order. Which transport service suits it best?
notes.back: C: TCP, because it is reliable and connection-oriented, with resequencing.
notes.explanation: TCP gives end-to-end reliability, resequencing and flow control, whereas the User Datagram Protocol is connectionless and adds none of these.
notes.source: RFC 1122, Requirements for Internet Hosts: Communication Layers, §1.1.3 Internet Protocol Suite
notes.sourceLicence: C · facts only, in our own words
notes.choices:
A) The IP layer alone, because it guarantees delivery
B) The User Datagram Protocol, because it is connectionless
C) TCP, because it is reliable and connection-oriented, with resequencing
D) Any transport service, because the hardware layer reorders data
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because a connectionless datagram service offers no reliability or reordering. A is wrong because the Internet Protocol is a datagram service with no end-to-end delivery guarantee. D is wrong because ordering and reliability are transport-layer services, not hardware-layer ones.

notes.front: Two merged charities want every system in each of their two office networks to talk securely to the other network over the internet, without installing anything on each laptop. Which VPN architecture fits?
notes.back: A: Gateway-to-gateway.
notes.explanation: That architecture protects communications between two specific networks, so gateways at each office do the protecting for all hosts behind them.
notes.evidence: Gateway-to-gateway. This architecture protects communications between two specific networks
notes.source: SP 800-77 Rev. 1, Guide to IPsec VPNs, Executive Summary
notes.choices:
A) Gateway-to-gateway
B) Remote access (host-to-gateway)
C) A transport-layer session per application
D) Host-to-host
notes.choicesExplained: D is wrong because host-to-host protects just two specific computers. B is wrong because remote access links individual hosts to one network and needs software on each host. C is wrong because it protects single sessions and needs each application to support it.
